A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AugServe. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original serving experiments, latency and goodput measurements, component ablations, and burst-arrival tests in Section 5 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v3 reports original comparative experiments, ablations, prediction-error tests, overhead measurements, and additional workload evaluations in Section 6 and Appendix D.

M1.justification: v1's phase-cost priority with an additive waiting-time adjustment becomes the descending value-density priority (1 + beta*w)/C in v3. Algorithm 1 also changes from explicit queue precedence to global ranking and greedy selection. The token budget now specifically counts reclaimable Swap/Discard contexts. These alter scheduling beyond renaming the retained prediction-and-feedback framework.

E1.justification: The underlying INFERCEPT-derived dataset, called Merge in v1, and ToolBench remain. v3 adds a distinct mixed serving scenario by disabling external calls for 50% of INFERCEPT requests while retaining their prompts and output lengths (Appendix D.1).

E2.justification: The main comparisons expand from vLLM and InferCept to include predicted-output-length SSJF. Appendix D.6 additionally evaluates a reimplementation of memory-based MARS on INFERCEPT and mixed workloads. These introduce substantially stronger scheduling comparators into reported evaluations.

E3.justification: v3 replaces OPT-13B on two A100 GPUs with Vicuna-13B and adds Llama-3-70B-Instruct on four A100 GPUs. It removes the fixed-2,000-request and relaxed-5x-SLO evaluations, introduces controlled prediction-noise and beta sweeps, and adds P99 TTFT for sensitivity analysis. It also specifies geometric-mean aggregation across settings; the primary latency SLOs remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a scheduling-only ablation, separating its contribution from dynamic batching, plus prediction-error injection, beta sensitivity, scheduling-overhead scaling, and GPU/CPU memory-occupancy analyses (Section 6; Appendix D). The latency breakdown expands to baselines and external-call time. Burst testing remains but loses ToolBench coverage, and relaxed-SLO sensitivity results are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added latency percentiles and prediction-noise experiments measure performance and robustness; geometric-mean benchmark summaries do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 revises existing results and adds SSJF/MARS, mixed-workload, 70B, and diagnostic results. For example, AugServe's reported OPT-13B/H800 goodput at 2 req/s and CV=1.5 changes from 1.15 in v1 Table 6 to 0.82 req/s in v3 Table 7. Fixed-2,000-request, relaxed-SLO, and TPOT result sets disappear. Changed methods and configurations preclude interpreting the revision as a uniform same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: v1's proposition about longer requests finishing earlier is removed. v3 adds formal service-segment definitions, a constrained scheduling objective, and an integral space-time cost formulation. Appendix E supplies a new 1/2-approximation proof for simplified fixed-cost knapsack selection using greedy packing plus the best feasible singleton; it explicitly excludes a guarantee for the full online scheduling problem.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains runtime-adaptive scheduling combined with dynamic batching for augmented inference. v3 emphasizes execution-state and cross-round awareness and revises headline performance claims: the abstract's goodput ranges of 4.7–33.1x and 3.3–13.2x become 6.5x and 4.7x, described as geometric means in the introduction.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations linking SSJF to GPU underutilization and InferCept to excessive CPU offloading, and explains degraded behavior at extreme beta values (Appendices D.3 and D.9). It also explicitly delineates the fixed-value, fixed-cost scope of its theoretical guarantee and leaves guarantees for online, evolving requests unresolved.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies 50-token prediction buckets, the 110M-parameter predictor, execution off the critical path, default beta=5e-5, and MARS reimplementation with a shared prediction interface. Conversely, it removes v1's 70/30 and 60/40 predictor training/evaluation splits and explicit phase-cost calculations, replacing the latter with more abstract formulations. Reproducibility documentation changes substantially in both directions.

R1.justification: v3 substantially sharpens positioning against MARS's per-round memory-based scheduling and newly cited BatchLLM's free-memory-based batching. v1 groups the MARS paper with length-based schedulers without this detailed distinction. Tool-agent references are also added. The substantive change concerns research positioning, beyond publication-metadata updates to retained references.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, motivation, design, evaluation, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces a separate Problem Formulation section, reorganizes the design narrative around state awareness, moves Related Work into Appendix C, and restructures the appendices into A–E. Author and terminology changes accompany this broader reorganization.

P2.justification: v3 combines v1 Figures 7–9 into a consolidated performance figure, adds lifecycle and system-architecture diagrams, converts the component ablation into a table, and introduces multiple diagnostic plots. Existing plots gain comparator series and revised axes or legends. The appendix changes from dense two-column presentation to full-width text, equations, tables, and figures.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the scheduling contribution through SSJF and reimplemented MARS comparisons, an independent scheduling ablation, prediction-error tests, and mixed-workload and 70B evaluations. These address important gaps in v1's predominantly FCFS-based comparisons and untested prediction robustness. Removing predictor splits, explicit cost calculations, and some earlier evaluations weakens reproducibility and coverage, while the new proof remains narrowly scoped. Overall, the stronger comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net quality improvement.
